analysis.one_liner: Makes Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac put more money into federal affordable housing funds each year.
analysis.headline: The bill more than doubled the share of mortgage-finance profits diverted to affordable housing funds, but died in committee without a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise the annual slice of money that mortgage giants Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac must set aside for two federal affordable housing funds — from 4.2 basis points to 10 basis points. That money goes to the Housing Trust Fund and the Capital Magnet Fund, which pay for building and preserving homes affordable to low-income families. The bill never advanced past its first day in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income renters and communities short on affordable housing, through bigger annual deposits into the Housing Trust Fund (which helps extremely low-income families) and the Capital Magnet Fund (which funds affordable housing and community development projects). Nonprofit and mission-driven housing developers who build with that money would also gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income renters and affordable housing developers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the mandatory annual allocation from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to the Housing Trust Fund and the Capital Magnet Fund from 4.2 basis points to 10 basis points — more than doubling the money set aside for affordable housing each year [S2][S3].

The Housing Trust Fund targets housing for extremely low-income families and the Capital Magnet Fund finances affordable housing and community development, so the new money flows directly to people priced out of the rental market [S2].
The funding is automatic and rises with mortgage volume, so it does not depend on yearly congressional appropriations that can be cut [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and the broader mortgage-finance system, which would set aside a larger slice of their business each year; some of that cost would likely flow to mortgage borrowers through slightly higher guarantee fees, spread thinly across millions of loans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage finance system and borrowers, thinly spread

drawbacks.text: The cost is passed into the mortgage market: a larger set-aside reduces the earnings of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and would likely be recovered through slightly higher guarantee fees paid by homebuyers with mortgages [S3].
The funding is tied to the mortgage market — it swings with interest rates and home-loan volume, so deposits into the housing funds rise and fall rather than staying stable [S2][S3].

The bill only changes a funding formula; it does not touch zoning, construction, or land-use barriers, so it subsidizes housing without directly increasing how much gets built where supply rules block it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and well-targeted: more than double the annual set-aside for programs that house extremely low-income families, at a cost spread thinly across the mortgage market. The main weakness is design — the money fluctuates with the mortgage cycle and the bill does nothing about the supply barriers that drive high housing costs in the first place. On balance a modest, low-cost pro-housing measure that never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Joyce Beatty introduced the bill on July 29, 2022, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, the committee that handles housing finance [S1][S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and the committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no floor consideration [S4][S5].
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023; bills not passed by then must start over from scratch in the next Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the mortgage-finance system kept the money that would have gone to the housing funds. A helpful bill died quietly at the first procedural step, with its sponsor left as its only supporter.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage finance system, which kept the money

for.name: Joyce Beatty
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the House Financial Services Committee; no cosponsors joined her.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.role: The House committee with jurisdiction over housing finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled action on it; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor, which is the normal path for a bill that has no committee action and no cosponsor base behind it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member of either party cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape was never tested.

industries.industry: Mortgage finance (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and lenders)
industries.note: The bill would have taken a larger annual slice — up from 4.2 to 10 basis points of their business — out of their earnings for affordable housing. Lenders and the two government-backed mortgage companies would bear the cost, likely passing part of it to borrowers through guarantee fees.

industries.industry: Affordable housing developers and community development financial institutions
industries.note: Larger deposits into the Housing Trust Fund and Capital Magnet Fund mean more grants and financing for building and preserving affordable homes, which is work these organizations carry out.
